cards.title: Internet vs. World Wide Web — Roads vs. Shops!
cards.takeaway: The Internet is the global network of cables/towers (the roads); the World Wide Web is the collection of websites running on it (the shops).
cards.body:
People often use *Internet* and *Web* as if they are identical, yet they are different:
- **The Internet:** The physical global network of cables, cell towers, and routers connecting devices (it also carries WhatsApp, email, and online games).
- **The World Wide Web (WWW):** Thewebsites and pages (`https://...`) you open inside a browser on top of the Internet!

cards.title: Browser, Server, and DNS — what happens when you visit a site
cards.takeaway: Your Browser (client) asks for a page, DNS looks up the server's number address, and the Server sends the website files back.
cards.body:
When you type `www.adaezefashion.com` into Chrome, three steps happen in less than a second:
1. **Client (your Browser):** Asks to view the website.
2. **DNS (Domain Name System):** Acts like the **phonebook of the internet** — turning the human name `adaezefashion.com` into a numeric **IP address** computers use to find the right machine.
3. **Server:** The remote computer storing the website's files, which sends the HTML, CSS, and images back to your browser!

check.prompt: What job does DNS do the moment you type a website name like `cea.ng` into your browser?

choices.text: It designs the colours and fonts of the page
It acts like a phonebook, translating the domain name into the server's numeric IP address
It deletes old files from your desktop

check.hint: Computers find each other by number (IP), while humans remember names — DNS bridges the two!
check.explanation: Spot on! DNS translates friendly web names into numeric IP addresses so your browser reaches the exact server.

cards.title: The 3 languages of every webpage: HTML, CSS & JavaScript
cards.takeaway: Think of a house: HTML is the block walls & structure, CSS is the paint & decoration, and JavaScript is the working switches & doors.
cards.body:
Every website on earth is built with three teammates:
- **HTML (Structure):** Put up the headings, paragraphs, buttons, and images — like the **bricks and rooms** of a house.
- **CSS (Style):** Controls colours, fonts, spacing, and mobile layout — like the **paint, tiles, and curtains**.
- **JavaScript (Behaviour):** Adds interactive actions like menus, carts, and pop-ups — like the **electricity and plumbing**!

check.prompt: In the house analogy of a webpage, what are the roles of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript?

choices.text: HTML = structure/content, CSS = visual styling/layout, JavaScript = interactive behaviour
HTML = internet cables, CSS = antivirus, JavaScript = printer driver
All three only change font colours
HTML = database, CSS = email, JavaScript = Wi-Fi

check.explanation: Exactly! HTML builds the content structure, CSS styles how it looks, and JavaScript makes it interactive.

cards.title: Project folders & why Relative Paths (`images/logo.png`) win
cards.takeaway: Keep everything inside one tidy project folder (`index.html`, `css/`, `images/`) and use relative paths so links still work online!
cards.body:
Always organise your website inside one clean project folder (`index.html`, `css/style.css`, `images/logo.png`).

**Why use a relative path like `images/logo.png` instead of `C:\Users\Ada\Desktop\logo.png`?**
Because when you upload your website to a real web server, **nobody on the internet has Ada's laptop C: drive**! A relative path (`images/logo.png`) works everywhere — on your laptop AND on the live web.

cards.title: Local file vs. Live online — hosting makes it public
cards.takeaway: Saving `index.html` on your laptop only lets YOU open it; for the world to visit it, you upload (deploy) the files to a web host/server.
cards.body:
Two gentle truths that save beginners hours of confusion: 1. **Save with `.html`, not `.txt`:** If you save your page as `home.txt`, the browser prints raw `

` code on screen! Rename it to `index.html` so the browser renders it as a real webpage. 2. **Local ≠ Online:** Building `index.html` on your PC keeps it only on your PC until you upload it to a **web host** (like GitHub Pages, Netlify, or Vercel).

check.prompt: You saved your first webpage as `home.txt`, and Chrome displays the raw HTML tags as plain text instead of a webpage. How do you fix it?

choices.text: Rename/save the file with the `.html` extension (e.g. `index.html` or `home.html`)
Delete all headings from the file

check.hint: Browsers check the file extension (`.txt` vs `.html`) to know whether to render HTML tags.
check.explanation: Right on! Changing `.txt` to `.html` tells the browser to interpret the tags and render a real webpage.

cards.title: Broken image icon on your page? Check these two things
cards.takeaway: Check spelling & capital letters (`Logo.PNG` ≠ `logo.png` on real servers!) and make sure the path is relative to your HTML file.
cards.body:
When an image refuses to show:
- Check exact file name and **lowercase spelling** (`images/logo.png`). Windows ignores capitals, whereas Linux web servers treat `Logo.png` and `logo.png` as two completely different files!
- Make sure the image actually sits inside your project's `images/` folder.

check.prompt: Why do web designers write `images/logo.png` instead of `C:\Users\Ada\Desktop\site\images\logo.png`?

choices.text: Because `C:\Users\Ada...` only exists on Ada's laptop and breaks as soon as the site goes online
Because HTML forbids capital letters anywhere in a file
Because PNG images only load on Sundays

check.hint: Think about what happens when another person's phone or a web server tries to find `C:\Users\Ada`!
check.explanation: 100% right! Relative paths (`images/logo.png`) travel cleanly inside your project folder from your laptop to any web server.
